stories.brief: Boris Schatz and the founding of Bezalel as a central chapter in Israeli art education.

sources.publisher: Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design
sources.title: About Bezalel
Ephraim Moshe Lilien: "The First Zionist Artist"

sources.publisher: Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design
sources.title: Milestones

storyBeats: Boris Schatz, a Lithuanian Jewish artist and sculptor, founded the Bezalel School in Jerusalem in 1906 as the first art school in modern-era Palestine.
He framed the school as a workshop-like arts-and-crafts institution rather than only a fine-arts academy, with an emphasis on training and applied work.
Schatz traveled to Jerusalem with Ephraim Moses Lilien in 1906, and Lilien helped establish the school’s visual identity and taught its first class.
The Bezalel project drew support from Zionist cultural networks, including Theodor Herzl’s backing as described by the academy itself.
After World War I, Schatz returned from exile and reopened the school in 1918, resuming instruction under changed circumstances.
Bezalel continued to add new departments and institutional functions in the 1920s, including a graphics department in 1921 and the National Bezalel Museum in 1925.
The school was hit by the global economic crisis and was temporarily closed in 1929 because of financial difficulties.
Schatz then traveled abroad to raise funds for the institution, continuing to work on Bezalel’s survival even after the closure.
Schatz died in Denver in 1932 during that fundraising effort, and his remains were later brought to Jerusalem and buried on the Mount of Olives.
Bezalel was reopened in 1935 as the New Bezalel under a new leadership structure, showing that Schatz’s institution survived beyond his lifetime.

stories.brief: Curt Wormann and the professionalization of Israeli librarianship after statehood.

sources.title: Book Diplomacy: Curt Wormann and the International Librarians
Curt Wormann and Felix Weltsch correspondence

storyBeats: Curt David Wormann was born in Berlin in 1900, studied at the universities of Berlin and Freiburg, and trained in librarianship before entering senior library work in Germany.
After the Nazi takeover and the racial laws in Germany, he emigrated with his wife to Palestine in 1934.
He first worked as an academic librarian at Sha’ar Zion Library in Tel Aviv, re-entering the profession in the local Hebrew public sphere rather than in an administrative post.
In 1947 he was appointed director of the Jewish National and University Library, a position he held until 1968.
As director, he worked with the Hebrew University and other librarians to connect Israeli librarianship to international professional networks, including UNESCO-related activity after 1949.

The National Library’s archival summary describes Wormann as one of the pioneers of Israeli librarianship, indicating that his work was understood institutionally as field-building rather than routine administration.
In 1956 he founded the School of Librarianship in Jerusalem, creating a training pipeline for a new Israeli professional class of librarians.
The NLI archive record notes that Wormann maintained correspondence and travel papers tied to international conferences and exchanges, showing an active transnational professional agenda.

By the time his directorship ended in 1968, the National Library listed him among its sequence of head librarians, and later institutional writing treated him as a central figure in the professionalization and institutionalization of Israeli librarianship.
The archive itself was deposited at the National Library in 1990, preserving the working record of his career for later research and institutional memory.

stories.brief: A woman goes to a neighborhood market with a friend to decide what to cook for a weekend dinner. They compare tomatoes, bread, and cheese, ask the vendor which fruit is sweetest right now, and realize one item is too expensive for their budget. After a short discussion, they choose a simpler menu, buy a few fresh ingredients, and split the cost. In the end, they leave with a small bag, a clear plan for dinner, and a note to come back earlier next time for better choices.

They compare two nearby places, ask which one is cheaper, and check whether the salad place still has tables. Maya realizes she already ate a snack and is not very hungry, so she suggests a lighter option instead.
